overview: This map period shows England under Henry VII and the early reign of Henry VIII, from 1492 to 1530. The Tudor dynasty had begun in 1485 and would last far beyond this interval. Royal marriage and court service shaped power, while farm leases, brewing, printed books and schooling shaped other lives. Bristol voyages reached North America, physicians obtained a charter to regulate their profession, and a printed fishing manual offered practical advice still easy to understand. The religious break with Rome came after this map period, not at England’s supposed disappearance in 1530.

periods.title: Henry VII’s England
periods.summary: The Tudor king consolidated his dynasty. Printing and Bristol’s Atlantic voyages connected England to wider networks of knowledge, commerce and ambition.

periods.title: Henry VIII’s early reign
periods.summary: Court life, new educational foundations and the College of Physicians developed under Henry VIII. Katherine of Aragon acted as regent in 1513; the break with Rome still lay ahead.

items.text: Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty after his victory in 1485; his son Henry VIII succeeded in 1509. The year 1492 is simply where this map record starts. It should not be mistaken for the founding of England or the Tudor family’s arrival.

John Cabot sailed from Bristol to North America in the Matthew in 1497. Research has also uncovered Italian financing for his ventures and Henry VII’s royal patent. These were voyages from England with international support; reaching a coast did not establish English rule over it.

Katherine of Aragon governed as regent in 1513 while Henry VIII campaigned in France. Her role during the Scottish invasion shows that a queen could exercise direct authority. Royal women’s work was more than producing heirs and appearing in portraits.

Bayleaf farmhouse in Kent had six rooms around a hall, with part of the building added in the early sixteenth century. Its tenants held a substantial farm on a long lease. This surviving house gives us a specific farming household to investigate, not a model for every rich or poor family.

Records name successive Bayleaf tenants around 1500-1540, including Thomas Wells, Edward Wells and Richard Scoriar. Their exact family relationships are uncertain. A shared surname is a clue, not permission to invent a family tree.

Brewing was household work as well as a trade. A museum reconstruction based on sources reaching back to 1502 uses grain, water and hops, which were becoming more popular in England. Heating, stirring and storing a batch took work long before anyone could lift a cup.

At court, family connections helped people find positions and marriage partners. Women served in the queen’s household, while powerful families sought advantageous alliances. These elite opportunities came with dependence on royal favor; they were not the normal life of a farm family.

The Eltham Ordinances of 1526 set rules for the royal household. Rank affected food, lodgings and access to the monarch. Court life could be glamorous, but it also came with a rulebook and a lot of people deciding which door you could enter.

sections.title: Schools, books and a writing sample

items.text: John Colet founded St Paul’s School in 1509 and entrusted its governance to London’s Mercers. Erasmus helped with planning and textbooks, and the statutes provided for 153 scholars. This was one influential school, not a system of schooling for every child.

Wynkyn de Worde printed a fishing treatise in 1496, part of the second edition of the Book of St Albans. Its traditional attribution to Juliana Berners is uncertain. Practical knowledge about tackle and fishing could circulate in print alongside religious and scholarly books.

A small sample of its English: “behynde a bushe that the fyshe se you not,” meaning “behind a bush so the fish cannot see you.” The advice is to keep out of sight and avoid casting a shadow over the water. Apparently the fish did not need to meet the angler before dinner.

In 1518 Henry VIII chartered the College of Physicians after an initiative by Thomas Linacre and five colleagues. It could license qualified practitioners and prosecute malpractice. This was a step in professional regulation, not the arrival of modern medicine or universal medical care.

Excavations at Hampton Court revealed toilet turrets from the manor that preceded Wolsey’s palace. Their waste emptied into the moat. One was incorporated into a building of the 1520s. A moat could be impressive scenery and a very poor place to go splashing.

Wolsey bought Hampton Court’s manor in 1514, and Henry VIII took over in 1529. Palace comfort depended on rank: important visitors received fine rooms, while servants found sleeping space around the kitchens. A palace’s luxury rested on other people’s labor.

ending.text: England continued after the map record ends in 1530. In 1534, Parliament’s Act of Supremacy declared Henry VIII head of the Church of England, breaking ecclesiastical ties with Rome. That later transformation changed religious and political life; it was not the extinction of the kingdom or its communities.
